Sanskrit is an ancient Indo-European language of India, the liturgical language of Hinduism and Buddhism, and the vehicle of vast classical literature. Systematically described by the grammarian Panini around the fourth century BCE, Sanskrit exemplifies linguistic structure and became central to nineteenth-century historical linguistics and the discovery of the Indo-European language family. Classical Sanskrit was the language of the Vedas, Hinduism's oldest scriptures, the epics the Mahabharata and Ramayana, and scientific and philosophical treatises. Panini authored the Ashtadhyayi, a remarkably concise and systematic grammar of Sanskrit—a model of linguistic description that influenced modern formal linguistics. William Jones, an English judge in India in seventeen eighty-six, observed striking similarities between Sanskrit, Latin, and Greek, proposing they shared a common ancestor, Proto-Indo-European. This insight launched historical comparative linguistics. Sanskrit's regular morphology and grammatical structure made it ideal for historical-comparative studies, and the language family it belongs to, Indo-European, contains most European and many Asian languages. Sanskrit is distinguished from Prakrit, the vernacular Middle Indo-Aryan languages, and from modern Hindi, Bengali, and others, which evolved from earlier Prakrit dialects. Sanskrit remains a liturgical language in Hinduism and Buddhism and is studied in universities worldwide for its grammar and as a window into ancient Indian civilization.
